feedback: If a learner routes blood from the lungs straight to the body, note that oxygenated blood returns to the LEFT side of the heart first and is re-pumped — that re-pressurising is the point of the second loop.
If a learner says the heart adds oxygen to the blood, correct: the lungs load the oxygen; the heart only pumps.
If a learner attributes pumping to the valves, clarify that valves only stop backflow — the muscular ventricle walls contract to pump.
If a learner treats the colour as literal, remind them it represents oxygenation state; deoxygenated blood is dark red, not blue.
activities.intendedInsight: Double circulation is a routing process: blood passes through the heart twice per full circuit, and the heart re-pressurises it between the lung loop and the body loop so it reaches the body at high pressure after being oxygenated. Valves prevent backflow; the pumping force comes from heart muscle, not valves.
learnerActions: Pump the heart and follow one blood drop all the way round, starting from the body: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → to the lungs → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → back to the body.

Watch (or mark, on paper) the drop's oxygenation change: it loads oxygen in the lungs (deoxygenated → oxygenated) and unloads it as body cells use it (oxygenated → deoxygenated) — note that colour represents oxygenation state, not literally blue blood.
Try to push blood backwards through a valve and observe that a valve blocks it.

Compare the two circuits with a 'single circulation' model version: route blood straight from the lungs to the body without an intermediate return to the heart, and describe what happens to its speed and pressure by the time it reaches the body.
State in one sentence WHY mammals use a double circuit, referring to the heart re-pressurising blood between the lung loop and the body loop.
activities.title: Drive the blood: tracing one drop through two loops

feedback: If the prediction and observation disagree, ask the learner to describe the valve's shape and how flow in one direction opens it while flow the other way presses it shut.
If a learner says the valve pumps or sets the heartbeat, separate the two: muscle contraction supplies the force; the valve only controls direction.
For the leaky-valve discussion: a leaky valve lets some blood flow backward (reduced efficiency), whereas a failed pump means the force to move blood is lost — both are problems, but different ones.
Remind learners that a physical specimen or water model is an approximation: it shows valve directionality but will not reproduce living pressures or flow.
activities.intendedInsight: Valves are passive one-way gates that prevent backflow; they are opened and closed by the pressure of blood the muscle moves, not a source of pumping themselves.
learnerActions: Before pouring, PREDICT which direction water will pass freely through a one-way valve model (or a valve in a fresh sheep/pig heart) and which direction will be blocked, and explain why.
Pour water through the valve in each direction and OBSERVE which way flows and which way is stopped.
Reconcile prediction with observation, stating in your own words what the valve does and what it does NOT do (it does not pump).
Discuss: if a valve became leaky, what problem would that cause, and why is that different from the pump (muscle) failing?
activities.title: Which way does water pass? Predict–observe with a valve

feedback: If a learner insists the pulmonary artery must carry oxygenated blood 'because all arteries do', show the route: it goes FROM the heart TO the lungs to collect oxygen — so the blood in it has not yet been oxygenated.
If a learner is unsure how many times a cell passes through the heart, have them retrace both loops: once before the lung loop and once before the body loop.

Reinforce that the direction-based definitions work for the circulation studied here, while the oxygenation rule has a standing exception at the pulmonary vessels (and also at the umbilical vessels before birth).
activities.intendedInsight: Arteries and veins are correctly defined by direction of flow, not oxygenation; the oxygenation shortcut breaks precisely at the pulmonary vessels. Vessel structure matches the pressure and function of each.
learnerActions: State the common shortcut rule: 'arteries carry oxygenated blood, veins carry deoxygenated blood.'

Apply it to the pulmonary artery and pulmonary vein, then check the actual blood each carries: the pulmonary artery carries DEOXYGENATED blood (heart to lungs); the pulmonary vein carries OXYGENATED blood (lungs to heart).
Rewrite the definition so it never fails: an artery carries blood AWAY from the heart; a vein carries blood TOWARD the heart — regardless of oxygenation.

Compare artery, vein and capillary structure and link each to its job: arteries have thick elastic walls for high pressure; veins have thinner walls and operate at low pressure, and many veins (especially in the limbs) have valves to prevent backflow; capillaries have one-cell-thick walls for exchange.
Trace a red blood cell from the vena cava all the way round until it returns, counting how many times it passes through the heart (twice per full circuit).
activities.title: Defining arteries and veins by direction, not oxygenation

feedback: Correct route order: body → vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle → aorta → body.

Diagnostic answer: the pulmonary vessels break the rule; the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood and the pulmonary vein carries oxygenated blood; define an artery as carrying blood away from the heart and a vein as carrying it toward the heart.
If a learner orders a single loop missing the separate lung circuit, return them to the drive-the-blood trace to re-establish the two loops.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure understanding means ordering the double-loop route correctly, defining vessels by direction, explaining valves and the septum, and justifying the left ventricle's thicker wall by its workload.
learnerActions: Put the chambers and vessels in the order a blood drop passes through them on a full double circuit.
Match each vessel type (artery, vein, capillary) to its distinguishing feature.
Explain why the left ventricle wall is thicker than the other chambers' walls.

Answer the diagnostic: a student writes 'arteries always carry oxygenated blood, veins always carry deoxygenated blood' — name the one pair of vessels where this breaks down, explain why it is wrong there, and give the correct direction-based definition.
activities.title: Check your understanding: sequence, match and explain
